questions.q: Why does this lesson say a solution that satisfies only one stakeholder type hasn't actually succeeded?
options: Because Salesforce contracts require sign-off from every department
Because each stakeholder type is accountable for a different outcome, and damaging one while satisfying another is a real failure, not a tolerable trade-off
Because stakeholders always have identical priorities in practice
Because only the business sponsor's opinion actually matters
questions.explain: A sponsor, end users, and a security/IT reviewer are each accountable for a different outcome. A design that pleases one while quietly damaging another (e.g., shipping fast but introducing real risk) hasn't succeeded just because one group is happy.

questions.q: A security reviewer asks "who else can see this field?" What underlying concern is that question most likely raising?
options: Whether the field name is spelled correctly
Whether the design respects least privilege
Whether the field will load quickly on mobile
Whether the field should be renamed for marketing purposes
questions.explain: A reviewer asking who can see a field is typically raising a least-privilege concern — whether access to that data is scoped appropriately — even though the question itself doesn't use that phrase.

questions.q: In the batch-job example, what changes between explaining the decision to a business sponsor versus a technical reviewer?
options: The underlying decision itself changes depending on the audience
Nothing is ever explained to the business sponsor
The framing changes to match what each audience needs to evaluate, while the underlying decision and trade-off stay identical
Only the technical reviewer is told about any trade-off at all
questions.explain: The decision and its real trade-off don't change — only how it's framed does. The sponsor hears about delivery timing and reliability; the technical reviewer hears about governor limits and error-handling, but it's the same underlying choice explained in each audience's own terms.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about two stakeholders wanting genuinely incompatible outcomes (e.g., speed vs. thorough security review)?
options: It means the project has failed and should be restarted
It is normal — both stakeholders can be doing their jobs correctly, and the architect's role is to make the trade-off visible rather than silently pick a side
The architect should always side with whichever stakeholder is more senior
It means one of the two stakeholders must be acting in bad faith
questions.explain: Disagreement between stakeholders with different accountabilities is expected, not a red flag. The architect's job is to surface the real trade-off to both parties so the actual decision-makers can choose with it in view, rather than letting the loudest voice win by default.

questions.q: In the lab's encryption example, what should stay identical across the two audience-framed explanations?
options: The vocabulary used in both versions, word for word
The actual underlying decision and trade-off, even though the framing differs
Nothing — a different decision should actually be made for each audience
The length of the explanation only
questions.explain: Audience-adjusted explanation means the framing changes to suit what each audience cares about, but the underlying decision itself — encrypting the field and accepting the reporting limitation that comes with it — stays exactly the same in both versions.
